title: FedSAC: Dynamic Submodel Allocation for Collaborative Fairness in Federated Learning

problem.claim: Federated learning needs collaborative fairness to encourage client participation by equitably distributing rewards according to individual contributions.

gap.claim: Existing methods primarily adjust gradient allocations but often overlook consistency across local models and the diverse requirements of high-contributing clients, reducing fairness and model accuracy.

contributions.claim: FedSAC is a federated learning framework using dynamic submodel allocation for collaborative fairness.
FedSAC introduces bounded collaborative fairness and implements it with a submodel allocation module that provides a theoretical fairness guarantee.
FedSAC develops dynamic aggregation to adaptively aggregate submodels, treat low-frequency neurons equitably, and improve overall model accuracy.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe FedSAC as a novel federated learning framework with dynamic submodel allocation for collaborative fairness.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments on three public benchmarks.
The authors report that FedSAC outperforms all baseline methods in fairness and model accuracy.
The authors report that source code is available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Collaborative fairness is presented as important for encouraging participation in federated learning.
Existing gradient-allocation approaches overlook local-model consistency and high-contributing clients, harming fairness and accuracy.
FedSAC addresses the gap through bounded collaborative fairness, submodel allocation, and dynamic aggregation.
The authors report superior fairness and model accuracy over baselines on three public benchmarks.
The authors position the work as supporting broader client participation in federated learning.

source_observation.claim: Tailoring rewards and submodel performance to client contributions is described as a way to preserve local-model consistency while supporting collaborative fairness.

interpretation.claim: Fairness mechanisms in collaborative learning may need to account for both contribution differences and model-structure consistency.

application.claim: When designing contribution-aware federated systems, consider allocating differentiated submodels and aggregating them dynamically.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these mechanisms generalize beyond the reported benchmarks or settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the three benchmarks, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not provide details of the convergence or fairness guarantees.
